name: Static PVs and PVCs
objective: CKA › Storage. Drill EVERY storage corner harder than the exam: StorageClasses (provisioner, reclaimPolicy, binding mode), static PVs with a retain reclaim policy, explicit static PVC binding, mounting a PVC, subPath mounts, the default-class annotation, dynamic provisioning via the default class, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Static PersistentVolume with Retain
questions.teach:
A **PersistentVolume (PV)** is cluster-scoped storage an admin pre-provisions (**static**). Set `capacity.storage`, `accessModes`, `storageClassName`, a backing source (here `hostPath`), and `persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain` so the PV (and its data) survives after its claim is deleted.

**Gotcha:** a PV's `persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy` is set on the **PV itself** — the StorageClass `reclaimPolicy` only applies to volumes the class *dynamically* provisions, not to this hand-made PV.
questions.prompt:
Create a PersistentVolume `pv-data`: capacity `1Gi`, accessModes `ReadWriteOnce`, `storageClassName: fast-local`, `hostPath` path `/mnt/data`, and `persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain`.

Target: `kubectl get pv pv-data` shows a 1Gi RWO Retain volume in class fast-local.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: pv-data
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 1Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: fast-local
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data
YAML

verification.description: PV pv-data: 1Gi, RWO, class fast-local, hostPath /mnt/data, reclaimPolicy Retain

questions.eli5:
Think of storage in a cluster like **lockers in a gym**.

A **PersistentVolume (PV)** is a real locker the gym manager (the admin) installs ahead of time. It has a fixed **size** (`capacity`), a rule for **how many people can use it at once** (`accessModes`), a **brand/tier** label (`storageClassName`, here `fast-local`), and a physical location — here a folder on the node's disk (`hostPath: /mnt/data`). Building the locker yourself up-front is called **static** provisioning.

The interesting setting is what happens **after someone stops renting the locker**. That's `persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy`:

- `Retain` means: when the renter leaves, **lock the locker and keep everything inside**. Nobody else gets it automatically, and the stuff is safe until an admin deals with it by hand.
- `Delete` would mean: when the renter leaves, **throw out the locker and everything in it**.

You picked `Retain` so the data survives even after the claim that used it is deleted. That is the safe, data-preserving choice.

**Watch out for:**

- The reclaim policy that matters here lives on the **PV itself** (`persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy`). A **StorageClass** also has a `reclaimPolicy`, but that one only applies to lockers the class **builds automatically** (dynamic) — it does **not** touch a hand-made PV like this one.
- `hostPath` stores data on **one specific node's** disk — fine for labs, but it is **not** real shared storage.
- `accessModes` on a PV describes its **capability**, not a live limit on connections.
- Get the units right: `1Gi` (binary) is not the same as `1G` (decimal).
questions.deepDive:
## Static PersistentVolumes — full rundown

### Mental model
A **PersistentVolume (PV)** is a piece of storage in the cluster, **cluster-scoped** (no namespace), that exists independently of any pod. **Static** provisioning means an **admin creates the PV by hand** ahead of time; a `PersistentVolumeClaim` (PVC) later binds to it. This is the opposite of **dynamic** provisioning, where a StorageClass creates PVs on demand.

A PV has three things that must line up with a claim before it can bind: **capacity**, **accessModes**, and **storageClassName**. It also carries a backing **source** (where the bytes actually live) and a **reclaim policy** (what happens to it after its claim goes away).

### Minimal static PV
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: pv-data
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 1Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: fast-local
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data
```
```bash
kubectl apply -f pv.yaml
kubectl get pv pv-data
kubectl get pv pv-data -o wide
kubectl describe pv pv-data
```

### Access modes
| Mode | Short | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ReadWriteOnce` | RWO | Mounted read-write by a **single node** (many pods on that node can share it) |
| `ReadOnlyMany` | ROX | Mounted read-only by **many nodes** |
| `ReadWriteMany` | RWX | Mounted read-write by **many nodes** |
| `ReadWriteOncePod` | RWOP | Read-write by **exactly one pod** cluster-wide (1.22+) |

> accessModes describe what the volume **can** do; they are not a runtime lock on connection count. A PVC binds only if the PV supports the mode the PVC asks for.

### Reclaim policies (set on the PV: `persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy`)
| Policy | On claim deletion | Data |
|---|---|---|
| `Retain` | PV goes to `Released`, **not** reused automatically | **kept**; admin must clean up / recreate PV manually |
| `Delete` | PV **and** backing storage deleted | **gone** |
| `Recycle` | *(deprecated)* basic `rm -rf` scrub then available | wiped |

With `Retain`, after you delete the PVC the PV status becomes **`Released`**. It will **not** rebind to a new PVC until an admin removes the stale `spec.claimRef` (e.g. `kubectl patch pv pv-data -p '{"spec":{"claimRef": null}}'`) or recreates the PV.

### PV phases
| Phase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Available` | free, not yet bound |
| `Bound` | bound to a PVC |
| `Released` | PVC deleted but PV not yet reclaimed (typical with `Retain`) |
| `Failed` | automatic reclamation failed |

### Common backing sources (exam-relevant)
- `hostPath` — a path on **one node's** filesystem (labs/single-node only; not portable).
- `local` — a local disk pinned to a node; **requires** `nodeAffinity` on the PV.
- `nfs` — a network share, supports RWX.
- `csi` — a CSI driver volume (cloud disks, etc.).

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **PV vs StorageClass reclaim policy:** `persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy` on the **PV** governs a hand-made PV. The StorageClass `reclaimPolicy` applies **only** to PVs that class **dynamically provisions** — it does nothing to a static PV.
- **PVs are cluster-scoped** — no `metadata.namespace`. Only PVCs are namespaced.
- **`Retain` leaves the PV `Released`, not `Available`.** It will not auto-rebind; clear `claimRef` or recreate it.
- **Capacity/accessModes/storageClassName must satisfy the claim**, or binding never happens.
- **Units:** `1Gi` = 2^30 bytes, `1G` = 10^9 bytes. Match what's requested.
- `hostPath` data is tied to whichever node the pod lands on — not shared storage.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl get pv                              # all PVs with capacity/modes/reclaim/status/class
kubectl get pv pv-data -o jsonpath='{.spec.persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy}'; echo
kubectl describe pv pv-data                 # events + claimRef
kubectl patch pv pv-data -p '{"spec":{"claimRef": null}}'   # free a Released PV
```

questions.title: Static PVC bound explicitly by volumeName
questions.teach:
A **PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)** is a namespaced request for storage. To bind a *specific* PV statically, set `spec.volumeName` to that PV's name; `accessModes`, `storageClassName`, and the requested size must still be satisfiable by the PV. When bound, the PVC shows status `Bound`.

**Gotcha:** if `volumeName` points at a PV whose class or access mode mismatches — or the request exceeds its capacity — the PVC stays `Pending`.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `storage-learn`, create PVC `pvc-data`: request `1Gi`, accessModes `ReadWriteOnce`, `storageClassName: fast-local`, bound explicitly to PV `pv-data` via `volumeName`.

Target: `kubectl -n storage-learn get pvc pvc-data` shows status `Bound` to `pv-data`.
questions.hint: PVC with `spec.volumeName: pv-data`, matching `storageClassName: fast-local`, `accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]`, and `resources.requests.storage: 1Gi`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: pvc-data
  namespace: storage-learn
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: fast-local
  volumeName: pv-data
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
YAML
kubectl -n storage-learn get pvc pvc-data

verification.description: PVC pvc-data is Bound to pv-data

questions.eli5:
Keeping the gym-locker picture: a **PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)** is the **rental slip** a user fills out to get a locker. It says "I need a locker at least this big, of this tier, that supports this kind of access." Kubernetes then finds a matching locker (PV) and **binds** the two together.

Normally you just describe what you want and let Kubernetes pick any matching locker. But here you want a **specific** locker. Setting `spec.volumeName: pv-data` on the claim is like writing *"give me locker #pv-data, exactly that one"* on the slip. That's **static binding by name**.

Even when you name the locker, the slip still has to be **compatible** with it: the size you request can't be bigger than the locker's capacity, the **tier** (`storageClassName`) has to match, and the **access mode** must be one the locker supports. When everything lines up, the PVC's status flips to **`Bound`**.

**Watch out for:**

- A PVC is **namespaced** — it lives inside `storage-learn`. A PV is **cluster-wide**. They still bind across that boundary.
- If `volumeName` points at a locker whose **class** or **access mode** doesn't match, or you ask for **more space than it has**, the PVC just sits `Pending` — no error popup, it simply never binds.
- Request size must be **≤** the PV's capacity. You'll often get the PV's **full** size regardless of a smaller request.
- Run `kubectl -n storage-learn describe pvc pvc-data` and read the **Events** to see why it won't bind.
- Binding is **one-to-one**: once a PV is bound to this claim, no other claim can grab it.
questions.deepDive:
## PersistentVolumeClaims & static binding — full rundown

### Mental model
A **PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)** is a **namespaced** request for storage: "I need X capacity, these access modes, this class." The **PV/PVC controller** matches the claim to a suitable **PV** and marks both `Bound`. Pods never reference a PV directly — they reference a **PVC**.

**Static binding** = you point the claim at one specific pre-made PV with `spec.volumeName`, instead of letting the controller choose.

### Static PVC bound by volumeName
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: pvc-data
  namespace: storage-learn
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: fast-local
  volumeName: pv-data          # <- bind to THIS PV
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
```
```bash
kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml
kubectl -n storage-learn get pvc pvc-data      # STATUS should be Bound, VOLUME pv-data
kubectl -n storage-learn describe pvc pvc-data # Events explain a stuck Pending
```

### What must match for a bind
| PVC field | Rule against the PV |
|---|---|
| `resources.requests.storage` | must be **≤** PV `capacity.storage` |
| `accessModes` | PV must **support** every mode requested |
| `storageClassName` | must **equal** the PV's `storageClassName` |
| `volumeName` (static) | names the exact PV; that PV must be `Available` (or already bound to this PVC) |
| `selector` (optional) | label selector the PV's labels must satisfy |

> A PVC may bind to a **larger** PV than requested — you get the whole PV. Binding is **1:1 and exclusive**: a bound PV cannot be claimed by anyone else.

### storageClassName values — the three cases
| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `fast-local` (a name) | bind only to PVs / provision via that class |
| **omitted** (field absent) | use the **default** StorageClass, if one exists |
| `""` (empty string) | explicitly **disable** dynamic provisioning — bind only to PVs that also have `storageClassName: ""` |

For **static** binding of a hand-made PV, set the **same** `storageClassName` on both PV and PVC (here `fast-local`).

### PVC phases
| Phase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Pending` | no matching/available volume yet (or waiting for a consumer with WaitForFirstConsumer) |
| `Bound` | tied to a PV |
| `Lost` | the bound PV was lost |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **PVC is namespaced; PV is cluster-scoped.** A pod + PVC must be in the **same namespace**; the PV is global.
- **Mismatch → silent `Pending`.** Wrong `storageClassName`, an access mode the PV lacks, or a request larger than capacity all leave the PVC `Pending` with a descriptive **Event** — never an apply-time error.
- **`volumeName` to an already-bound/`Released` PV won't bind.** The PV must be `Available`.
- **`storageClassName` is immutable** once set — fix a wrong class by deleting and recreating the PVC.
- **PVCs can only grow, never shrink**, and only if the StorageClass has `allowVolumeExpansion: true`.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n storage-learn get pvc                 # NAME STATUS VOLUME CAPACITY ACCESSMODES STORAGECLASS
kubectl get pv pv-data                           # confirm CLAIM points back to the PVC
kubectl -n storage-learn describe pvc pvc-data   # Events: why Pending
```

questions.title: Mount the PVC in a pod
questions.teach:
A pod consumes a PVC via `spec.volumes[].persistentVolumeClaim.claimName`, then a container mounts it with `volumeMounts[].mountPath`. Give busybox `sleep 3600` so the pod stays `Running`.

**Gotcha:** if the PVC is `Pending` or missing, the pod never leaves `Pending` — mounting an unbound claim blocks scheduling.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `storage-learn`, create pod `app` (`busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) that mounts PVC `pvc-data` at `/data`.

Target: pod `app` reaches `Running` with `pvc-data` mounted at `/data`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: storage-learn
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: data
      mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: data
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: pvc-data
YAML
kubectl -n storage-learn wait --for=condition=Ready pod/app --timeout=60s

verification.description: pod app is Running with pvc-data mounted at /data

questions.eli5:
You've got a rental slip for a locker (the **PVC**). Now you actually want to **use** it inside your pod.

In Kubernetes this takes **two linked pieces**:

1. **`spec.volumes`** on the pod — this is you saying *"this pod has a storage slot, and I'm plugging the locker named `pvc-data` into it."* You give the slot a short nickname (like `data`).
2. **`volumeMounts`** on the container — this is you saying *"inside my container, make that slot show up at the folder `/data`."* You refer to the slot by the same nickname.

So the pod **claims** the storage, and the container **mounts** it to a path. Anything the app writes to `/data` lands in the real locker and survives the container restarting.

The `sleep 3600` command just keeps the little busybox container alive and doing nothing for an hour, so the pod stays `Running` long enough to inspect.

**Watch out for:**

- The **name must match**: the nickname in `volumes[].name` has to be the exact string in `volumeMounts[].name`. A typo means the mount silently refers to nothing and the pod won't start.
- If the PVC is still `Pending` or doesn't exist, the **pod never starts** — it sticks in `Pending`/`ContainerCreating` because it can't attach storage that isn't bound yet.
- The PVC and the pod must be in the **same namespace** (`storage-learn`).
- Mounting onto a path that already has files **hides** whatever was there while the volume is mounted.
questions.deepDive:
## Mounting a PVC in a pod — full rundown

### Mental model
Consuming storage in a pod is always **two halves** that are wired together by a **name**:

1. **`spec.volumes[]`** — declares a volume on the **pod** and says what backs it (here a `persistentVolumeClaim`).
2. **`spec.containers[].volumeMounts[]`** — mounts that volume into a **container** at a `mountPath`.

The two are linked because `volumeMounts[].name` must equal `volumes[].name`.

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: storage-learn
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: data            # must match volumes[].name
      mountPath: /data      # path inside the container
  volumes:
  - name: data
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: pvc-data    # the PVC to consume
```
```bash
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
kubectl -n storage-learn get pod app -o wide
kubectl -n storage-learn exec app -- sh -c 'echo hi > /data/x && cat /data/x'
```

### Key fields
| Field | On | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `volumes[].name` | pod | nickname linking volume ↔ mount |
| `volumes[].persistentVolumeClaim.claimName` | pod | which PVC to attach |
| `volumeMounts[].name` | container | must equal `volumes[].name` |
| `volumeMounts[].mountPath` | container | where it appears in the container FS |
| `volumeMounts[].readOnly` | container | mount read-only (bool) |
| `volumeMounts[].subPath` | container | mount only a sub-dir/file (next lesson) |

### How binding and scheduling interact
- A pod referencing a PVC will **not start** until that PVC is `Bound`. An unbound/`Pending` PVC blocks the pod at `Pending` → `ContainerCreating`.
- With a `WaitForFirstConsumer` StorageClass, this is the reverse trigger: scheduling the pod is what **causes** the PVC to bind.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Name mismatch** between `volumes[].name` and `volumeMounts[].name` is the #1 error — the pod won't validate/start.
- **PVC must be in the same namespace as the pod.** PVCs are namespaced; there is no cross-namespace claim.
- **Missing/Pending PVC → pod Pending.** `kubectl describe pod` Events: `persistentvolumeclaim "..." not found` or `waiting for first consumer`.
- **Mounting over a non-empty directory hides** the existing files for the life of the mount (use `subPath` to avoid clobbering).
- **RWO** means one **node**: multiple pods can share an RWO volume only if they land on the **same node**.
- A **container** that exits (no `sleep`/long process) makes the pod `Completed`/`CrashLoopBackOff`; keep busybox alive with `sleep`.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n storage-learn get pod app -o wide
kubectl -n storage-learn describe pod app | sed -n '/Volumes/,/Events/p'
kubectl -n storage-learn exec app -- df -h /data
```

questions.title: subPath: mount one sub-directory of a volume
questions.teach:
`volumeMounts[].subPath` mounts a single file or sub-directory of a volume instead of its root — handy to share one PVC across containers without them clobbering each other's paths. The subPath is created inside the volume if it doesn't exist.

**Gotcha:** `subPath` is a field on the **volumeMount**, not the volume; a plain `mountPath` with no `subPath` would expose the whole volume.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `storage-learn`, create pod `sub-app` (`busybox:1.36`, `sleep 3600`) that uses PVC `pvc-data` but mounts only its sub-directory `logs` at `/var/log/app` using `subPath: logs`.

Target: pod `sub-app` mounts `pvc-data` at `/var/log/app` with `subPath` = `logs`.
questions.hint: Same `persistentVolumeClaim` volume as before, but the `volumeMounts` entry adds `subPath: logs` alongside `mountPath: /var/log/app`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: sub-app
  namespace: storage-learn
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: data
      mountPath: /var/log/app
      subPath: logs
  volumes:
  - name: data
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: pvc-data
YAML

verification.description: sub-app mounts pvc-data at /var/log/app with subPath logs

questions.eli5:
Imagine a volume is a whole **filing cabinet** with several drawers: `logs`, `config`, `cache`. Normally when you mount the volume, the container sees the **entire cabinet** at the mount path.

**`subPath`** is you saying: *"don't give me the whole cabinet — just open the `logs` **drawer** and show me that at `/var/log/app`."* The container sees only the contents of that one drawer, not the rest.

Why bother? Because often several containers (or several apps) want to share **one** PVC but each keep to its **own corner** without stepping on the others. One uses `subPath: logs`, another uses `subPath: config`, and they both live in the same cabinet peacefully. If the drawer doesn't exist yet, Kubernetes **creates it** inside the volume for you.

**Watch out for:**

- `subPath` is a field on the **volumeMount**, not on the volume. Put it next to `mountPath`, not down in the `volumes:` section.
- Leave `subPath` off and you mount the **whole** volume at the path — the default, whole-cabinet behavior.
- `subPath` is a **relative** path *inside* the volume (`logs`, `logs/app`), never an absolute host path like `/mnt/...`.
- A classic pitfall: **ConfigMap/Secret updates don't auto-refresh** in a container when mounted via `subPath` — they stay frozen at the version present when the pod started. (For plain data volumes this isn't an issue, but remember it for config.)
- Use `subPathExpr` if you need environment-variable substitution in the path.
questions.deepDive:
## subPath mounts — full rundown

### Mental model
By default, mounting a volume exposes its **root** at `mountPath`. **`subPath`** mounts only a **single sub-directory or file within** the volume instead, so one volume can be carved up and shared cleanly between containers or between mount points — without each consumer seeing (or overwriting) the others' data.

`subPath` is a field on the **`volumeMount`**, not on the volume.

### The manifest
```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: data
      mountPath: /var/log/app   # where it appears
      subPath: logs             # mount only <volume>/logs here
  volumes:
  - name: data
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: pvc-data
```
Here `/var/log/app` inside the container maps to the `logs/` directory **inside** `pvc-data`. The `logs` directory is **created automatically** in the volume if absent.

### subPath vs subPathExpr
| Field | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `subPath` | static relative path | e.g. `logs`, `logs/app` |
| `subPathExpr` | path with `$(VAR)` expansion | uses container env vars (e.g. `$(POD_NAME)`); **mutually exclusive** with `subPath` |

```yaml
    env:
    - name: POD_NAME
      valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name } }
    volumeMounts:
    - name: data
      mountPath: /data
      subPathExpr: $(POD_NAME)     # per-pod sub-directory in a shared volume
```

### Classic use cases
- One PVC, **multiple containers**, each pinned to its own sub-dir (`logs`, `cache`, `config`).
- Mounting **one key** of a ConfigMap/Secret as a file into an existing directory **without hiding** the rest of that directory.
- Per-pod or per-replica sub-directories via `subPathExpr`.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`subPath` lives on the volumeMount**, beside `mountPath` — not under `volumes:`.
- **Omit it → the whole volume** is mounted at `mountPath` (default behaviour).
- **Relative path only.** It's relative to the volume root (`logs`), never an absolute host path.
- **ConfigMap/Secret auto-update does NOT work through `subPath`.** A `subPath`-mounted config file is frozen at the value present when the pod started; updates propagate only to **full** (non-subPath) mounts. This is a favourite trap.
- **`subPath` + `subPathExpr` are mutually exclusive** on the same mount.
- Mounting a `subPath` into a directory that already has files **hides** those files just like a normal mount.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n storage-learn get pod sub-app -o jsonpath=\
'{.spec.containers[0].volumeMounts[0].subPath}'; echo        # -> logs
kubectl -n storage-learn exec sub-app -- sh -c 'echo x > /var/log/app/a && ls /var/log/app'
```
